notes.wange: Mon, ma or mes, depending on the noun: mon père, ma mère, mes enfants.
notes.jjajja: A grandmother is une grand-mère, a grandfather un grand-père.
notes.abaana: Enfant(s) is masculine or feminine depending on the child: un enfant, une enfant.
notes.omusomesa: For a woman: la professeure, or simply la prof.
notes.emmere: Feminine: la nourriture. People also say à manger: Je veux à manger.
notes.oluganda: Language names are masculine and lower case: le luganda, le français.
notes.wake: Son, sa or ses: it agrees with the noun, not with the owner. Sa mère is “his mother” or “her mother”.

guidebook.intro: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and the little words around it, like “the”, “a” and “my”, change to match.

tips.title: Le or la: every noun has a gender
body: Masculine nouns take **le** (the) and **un** (a): **le livre, un livre**. Feminine nouns take **la** and **une**: **la tasse, une tasse**. Before a vowel both become **l’**: **l’enfant, l’eau**.
The gender of things has to be learned with the word, so always learn **la table**, not just **table**. People follow their sex: **le père, la mère**.

tips.title: Plurals: les, des and a silent -s
body: In the plural, **le** and **la** both become **les**, and **un, une** become **des**: **les enfants, des livres**. Most nouns add **-s**, but you don’t hear it: **livre** and **livres** sound the same. The little word in front tells you it’s plural.
“My” has three forms: **mon** (masculine), **ma** (feminine) and **mes** (plural): **mon livre, ma tasse, mes livres**.

tips.title: Je veux de l’eau: “some”
body: For things you don’t count, French adds **du, de la, de l’**: **Je bois du thé** (I drink tea), **Je veux de l’eau** (I want water). English often leaves this out, but French needs it.
Verbs change with the person: **je mange, je bois, je lis, j’apprends**. You’ll meet the other persons step by step.

culture.title: Family words
body: **Grand-mère** and **grand-père** become **mamie** and **papi** at home. **Tonton** and **tata** (uncle, aunt) are used for any older family friend in much of francophone Africa.
